title: Placebo effect in the rat.
abstract: Scopolamine hydrobromide disrupts the learned behavior of rats in a predictable manner. Physiological saline mimics to some extent the effect of the drug when the two substances are alternately administered in a series of injections. This placebo effect appears to be an instance of simple Pavlovian conditioning.

screening.rationale: Animal experiment explicitly investigated a placebo effect (saline mimicking scopolamine) and interpreted it as Pavlovian conditioning, meeting criterion 3 for mechanistic animal models.

classification.summary: Found that saline injections began to mimic scopolamine's disruption of learned behavior in rats after alternated administrations, suggesting a Pavlovian conditioned placebo effect.
classification.key_finding: Saline partially reproduced scopolamine-induced behavioral disruption after alternating drug and saline, consistent with conditioning.

title: Controlled trials: nuisance or necessity?
abstract: Placebos can mimic in many ways the characteristics of active drugs. The importance of placebo controls in clinical trials in the evaluation of therapeutic efficacy and side action liability of drugs is exemplified by specific examples from human experimentation. It is concluded that controlled trials will prevent many of the errors inherent in uncontrolled therapeutic observations.

screening.rationale: Paper focused on the role and methodology of placebo controls in clinical trials (placebo science/methodology), so it meets inclusion criterion 5.

classification.summary: Discussed the importance of placebo controls in clinical trials and argued they prevent errors inherent in uncontrolled therapeutic observations.
